title: Ezekiel 47:13–23
context: The Lord GOD now speaks to the prophet about the borders of the land, to be divided among the twelve tribes, with “Joseph shall have two portions,” and each tribe inheriting “one as well as another” because the LORD swore to give it to their fathers. The borders run from the great sea on the west to the Jordan on the east, and from the north near Hamath and Damascus to the south from Tamar to the waters of Meriboth Kadesh, broadly echoing the borders in Numbers 34, though many of the places, such as Hethlon, Zedad, Berothah, Hazar Enon, and Tamar, are identified with varying confidence. The section closes with aliens who live among Israel and father children there receiving an inheritance “as the native-born,” which both traditions read as shared ground about the LORD’s welcome of outsiders into his people.

verses.text: The Lord GOD says: “This shall be the border by which you shall divide the land for inheritance according to the twelve tribes of Israel. Joseph shall have two portions.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says, “This shall be the border by which you shall divide the land for inheritance according to the twelve tribes of Israel. Joseph shall have two portions.” Arminian readers note that “the Lord GOD” renders Adonai joined to the divine name.

Joseph’s double share recalls Genesis 48:5.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the land divided according to God’s promise to the tribes.

Shared ground: both traditions read the two portions as Ephraim and Manasseh, named in 48:4–5, and agree that the twelve-tribe division pictures a reunited people (cf. 37:22).

verses.text: You shall inherit it, one as well as another; for I swore to give it to your fathers. This land will fall to you for inheritance.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You shall inherit it, one as well as another; for I swore to give it to your fathers.” Arminian readers note the equal shares and the grounding in God’s oath.

The promise to the patriarchs is remembered (cf. Gen 15:18).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the land given on the basis of God’s sworn promise rather than the tribes’ merit.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD keeps his word to Abraham’s descendants, and that the equal division contrasts with the inequalities of earlier history.

verses.text: “This shall be the border of the land: “On the north side, from the great sea, by the way of Hethlon, to the entrance of Zedad;
verses.arminianNotes:
“This shall be the border of the land,” beginning on the north side “from the great sea, by the way of Hethlon, to the entrance of Zedad.” Arminian readers note that the description begins with the north.

Zedad also appears in Numbers 34:8.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the border drawn in continuity with the earlier promise of the land.

Shared ground: both traditions hold the location of Hethlon and Zedad with care and read the list as defining the whole land given to the tribes.

verses.text: Hamath, Berothah, Sibraim (which is between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath), to Hazer Hatticon, which is by the border of Hauran.
verses.arminianNotes:
The border runs by “Hamath, Berothah, Sibraim,” to “Hazer Hatticon, which is by the border of Hauran.” Arminian readers note the northern boundary near Damascus and Hamath.

Several of these places are not securely identified.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold the identifications lightly.

Shared ground: both traditions read the list as part of a careful description of the land, without resting any doctrine on the exact locations.

verses.text: The border from the sea shall be Hazar Enon at the border of Damascus; and on the north northward is the border of Hamath. This is the north side.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The border from the sea shall be Hazar Enon at the border of Damascus.” Arminian readers note that the north border is summed up here.

The verse ends, “This is the north side.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the northern limit fixed by the LORD’s word.

Shared ground: both traditions hold the location of Hazar Enon with care and read the verse as completing the northern boundary.

verses.text: “The east side, between Hauran, Damascus, Gilead, and the land of Israel, shall be the Jordan; from the north border to the east sea you shall measure. This is the east side.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The east side, between Hauran, Damascus, Gilead, and the land of Israel, shall be the Jordan.” Arminian readers note that the Jordan forms the eastern boundary.

The land east of the Jordan, settled by some tribes earlier, is not included here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the difference from the earlier settlement in Joshua without harmonizing it.

Shared ground: both traditions read the border as part of a new allotment that differs in places from the earlier one.

verses.text: “The south side southward shall be from Tamar as far as the waters of Meriboth Kadesh, to the brook, to the great sea. This is the south side southward.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The south side southward shall be from Tamar as far as the waters of Meriboth Kadesh, to the brook, to the great sea.” Arminian readers note the southern boundary.

The name recalls the waters of Meribah in the wilderness story.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the border recalling Israel’s history in the desert.

Shared ground: both traditions hold the locations of Tamar and the brook with care and read the verse as completing the southern limit.

verses.text: “The west side shall be the great sea, from the south border as far as opposite the entrance of Hamath. This is the west side.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The west side shall be the great sea, from the south border as far as opposite the entrance of Hamath.” Arminian readers note that the sea forms the western boundary.

The four sides are now complete.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the land fully defined by God’s word.

Shared ground: both traditions read the completed borders as a sign that the promised inheritance is clearly marked and secure.

verses.text: “So you shall divide this land to yourselves according to the tribes of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So you shall divide this land to yourselves according to the tribes of Israel.” Arminian readers note that the people themselves are to carry out the division.

The instruction prepares for chapter 48.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the division as obedience to God’s arrangement.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a transition from the borders to the inclusion of aliens and then the tribal allotments.

verses.text: You shall divide it by lot for an inheritance to you and to the aliens who live among you, who will father children among you. Then they shall be to you as the native-born among the children of Israel. They shall have inheritance with you among the tribes of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The land is to be divided “for an inheritance to you and to the aliens who live among you.” Arminian readers note that they “shall be to you as the native-born among the children of Israel.”

The welcome echoes Leviticus 19:34.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s people including outsiders who live among them (cf. Isa 56:6–7).

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a generous inclusion of sojourners in the inheritance, a picture of the LORD’s welcome.

verses.text: In whatever tribe the stranger lives, there you shall give him his inheritance,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In whatever tribe the stranger lives, there you shall give him his inheritance,” says the Lord GOD. Arminian readers note that the stranger’s share is given where he lives.

Inclusion is practical, not merely stated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the inheritance extended to those who join themselves to Israel.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the closing words of the border section affirm the place of outsiders among God’s people.
